w: What's tested Dr. Herr's study guide for this lecture: the common disorders of the vulva, vagina and cervix; telling neoplastic lesions from non-neoplastic ones; the important infectious causes (infectious vaginitis: Candida and Trichomonas; HPV); the relationship between HPV and cervical neoplasia; and the age-related patterns of the tumors (sarcoma botryoides in little girls, squamous cell carcinoma in women of reproductive age, the HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma and the aggressive endometrial carcinoma in older women). Key terms: lichen sclerosus, condyloma acuminatum, sarcoma botryoides, HPV, cervical neoplasia, infectious vaginitis The cervix's transformation zone, where the glandular and squamous epithelia meet and "fight": constantly inflamed, open to HPV infection, and where cervical cancer arises; the precursors (low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions), 90 percent linked to HPV, and the koilocyte Lichen sclerosus, where Dr. Dal Zotto paused "because this is important": the one non-infectious inflammatory disorder that can lead to carcinoma, the HPV-independent squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva in older women Lichen planus, "because you're going to be dentists": vulvar and oral lesions together point to it The endometrium's two carcinomas, the leiomyoma (very common, abnormal bleeding), and the breast: ductal versus lobular carcinoma, in situ versus invasive, Paget disease of the nipple, the receptors (estrogen, progesterone, HER2) and gynecomastia What the lecture said you don't need: the details of the new cervical screening (know only that management is now risk-based), the classification of ovarian tumors (know that most are epithelial, and that ovarian cancer is lethal), and how ductal and lobular carcinoma in situ differ under the microscope 1 HPV and cervical neoplasia: cancer arises in the transformation zone, where the glandular and squamous epithelia "fight" and stay inflamed and open to HPV; the precursors are squamous intraepithelial lesions, low grade (can regress) or high grade (progress), about 90 percent HPV-linked, marked by the koilocyte, in situ until they invade the stroma Study guide + recording · 9 questions in the bank Know this Cervical cancer arises in the transformation zone, where the endocervix's glandular epithelium meets the ectocervix's squamous epithelium. The fighting of epithelia keeps the transformation zone inflamed and open to HPV, which can progress to carcinoma. Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions can regress; high-grade ones progress. About 90 percent are linked to HPV. Where the two epithelia meet is the transformation zone, the junction of the epithelia. Through the reproductive years the glandular epithelium of the endocervix tries to grow out onto the ectocervix and the squamous epithelium tries to grow into the canal: they collide, "what we call the fighting of epithelia." So the transformation zone is constantly inflamed and injured, and that chronic inflammation makes it susceptible to infection, above all HPV, the virus that affects the whole genital tract in women and men. That is why the transformation zone is where cervical cancer arises. The precursors of cervical cancer are squamous intraepithelial lesions (SIL; also called cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN), because they affect the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix, as penile intraepithelial lesions do on the penis. They are low grade (LSIL), which progress slowly and can regress, or high grade (HSIL), which are less likely to regress and more likely to progress to carcinoma. About 90 percent are linked to HPV, in the reproductive years. 2 Lichen sclerosus, where the lecture paused "because this is important": an atrophic epithelium over dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, a parchment-like vulva; the one non-infectious inflammatory disorder that leads to carcinoma, the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of older women Study guide + recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this Of lichen simplex chronicus, lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, only lichen sclerosus leads to carcinoma. The epithelium is completely atrophic, and the hallmark is extensive dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, pink material in the dermis. The vulva looks very smooth, like parchment paper or cellophane. Lichen sclerosus itches, so the patient scratches, and lichen simplex chronicus can form on top of it. "Lichen sclerosus is the single non-infectious inflammatory disorder that can lead to carcinomas." HPV-independent: in older women, over 60, associated with lichen sclerosus. That is why lichen sclerosus has to be diagnosed in time and treated, not left until a squamous cell carcinoma develops. 3 Infectious vaginitis: Candida (pseudohyphae, little sticks, a lot of inflammation) and Trichomonas vaginalis (a sexually transmitted protozoan that looks like a squamous cell with prolongations), against non-infectious atrophic vaginitis in older women Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this Infectious vaginitis: Candida (pseudohyphae, little sticks) and Trichomonas vaginalis (a sexually transmitted protozoan with prolongations). Non-infectious: atrophic vaginitis in older women. Candida, a fungus: its pseudohyphae look like "little sticks" in the cytology, with a lot of inflammation; very frequent. Trichomonas vaginalis, a sexually transmitted protozoan, a very common cause of vaginitis: easy to diagnose in cytology, because it looks like a squamous cell but has cytoplasmic prolongations (pseudopods). Atrophic vaginitis, non-infectious, very common in older women, not related to any infectious agent. 4 Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types; benign, finger-like and wart-like, with koilocytes, anywhere on the anogenital tract Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank Know this Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, benign, finger-like and wart-like, with koilocytes. Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma: HPV 16 and 18, or, in women over 60, lichen sclerosus. As on the penis, condyloma acuminatum can affect any part of the anogenital tract. It is associated with HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types: a benign condition, though it can be painful or ulcerate. It forms finger-like, exophytic, wart-like (verruciform) lesions, big or small, and under the microscope it shows koilocytes, because it is HPV. 5 The age patterns of the tumors: sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) in girls under 5, with a good prognosis if treated in time; squamous cell carcinomas in women of reproductive age; the HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma and the aggressive endometrial carcinoma in older women Study guide + recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) in girls under 5, with a good prognosis if treated in time; squamous cell carcinomas in women of reproductive age. In very young girls, under 5, a different tumor is prevalent: sarcoma botryoides, an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, a very primitive tumor. It has a good prognosis if it is found in time and treated with surgery and chemotherapy. "So know that there are certain tumors that affect the girls, and usually the squamous cell carcinomas affect the women in reproductive age." Girls under 5 Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) of the vagina Women of reproductive age Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and vagina, HPV-related; endometrioid adenocarcinoma in younger women with excess estrogen Older women HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (over 60, lichen sclerosus); the aggressive endometrial carcinoma (over 65) 6 The common disorders of the vulva, and neoplastic versus non-neoplastic: lichen simplex chronicus (thickened, leathery, from scratching), lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are inflammatory; squamous intraepithelial lesions, VaIN, squamous cell carcinoma and sarcoma botryoides are neoplastic Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Dal Zotto's lecture. Know HPV and the cervix (the transformation zone, the low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, 90 percent HPV, the koilocyte), the infectious vaginitis pair (Candida's pseudohyphae; Trichomonas, a sexually transmitted protozoan with prolongations) against atrophic vaginitis, the vulva's lichens (lichen sclerosus leads to HPV-independent carcinoma), condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6 and 11, benign), and the ages: sarcoma botryoides in girls under 5, squamous carcinomas in the reproductive years, lichen sclerosus carcinoma in older women. A thickening of the vulvar skin (a squamous mucosa) from continuous scratching and rubbing. In older patients, an atrophic epithelium with less estrogen becomes itchy and the patient scratches; or a psychological problem leads to scratching. The epithelium thickens, with hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis and acanthosis, and the skin looks leathery. It is a reaction to many conditions that cause pruritus. Cervix Inflammation of the transformation zone Low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions; squamous cell carcinoma Vagina Vaginitis: Candida, Trichomonas, atrophic Vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia, squamous cell carcinoma; sarcoma botryoides in girls under 5 Vulva Lichen simplex chronicus, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus; condyloma acuminatum (a benign HPV lesion) Squamous intraepithelial lesions; squamous cell carcinoma (HPV 16 and 18, or lichen sclerosus) 7 Lichen planus, "because you're going to be dentists": vulvar and oral erosions together; lymphocytes in the dermis; a fresh biopsy (not formalin) for immunofluorescence; steroids Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank Know this Lichen planus: oral and vulvar erosions together; a fresh biopsy (not in formalin) for immunofluorescence; steroids. "You must know about this, because you're going to be dentists." Lichen planus is an inflammatory disorder of the oral mucosa and also of the vulva, where its diagnosis is often delayed because it isn't recognized. If a patient has vulvar and oral lesions, it is most likely lichen planus. It is postulated to be an autoimmune, cell-mediated disorder; it causes erosions, sometimes very painful and ulcerated, in the vulva and the mouth, with many inflammatory cells, especially lymphocytes, in the dermis. The diagnosis is easy: send the biopsy to the pathology laboratory fresh, not in formalin, for immunofluorescence, which shows no immune complexes and a deposit of fibrin. The patient is treated with steroids. 8 Cervical cancer and its prevention: fourth in women worldwide (breast is first), less common in the United States thanks to Pap screening (a fourth of women lack access), the HPV vaccine (decades to show its full benefit), and management now based on each patient's risk Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide; breast cancer is first. It is less frequent in the United States because screening (Papanicolaou cytology, the Pap test) finds the premalignant lesions early and is well established and widespread. Still, about a fourth of U.S. women can't get or don't have access to screening, and the lecture said cervical cancer will develop in about 5 percent of those not screened correctly. Effective screening reduces both the incidence and the mortality significantly. 9 The two endometrial carcinomas, "just know": endometrioid adenocarcinoma (estrogen excess, obesity, estrogen without progesterone; well differentiated, less aggressive, younger women) and the aggressive type of women over 65 Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Endometrioid adenocarcinoma: estrogen excess (obesity, estrogen without progesterone), well differentiated, less aggressive, younger women. The other type: over 65, unlike endometrium, more aggressive. Endometrioid adenocarcinoma, which looks somewhat like normal endometrium (hence the name): tied to estrogen stimulation, in obese patients with excess estrogen or women taking estrogen without progesterone to counteract it. It is well differentiated and less aggressive, and the patients are usually younger (the lecture said premenopausal or perimenopausal). 10 Breast carcinoma: DCIS needs treatment, LCIS is now considered benign; invasive ductal carcinoma forms glands, invasive lobular grows in single files; Paget disease of the nipple means a carcinoma underneath; the prognosis rests on size, nodes and the estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2 Flagged in the recording · 7 questions in the bank Know this Breast carcinoma's prognosis: type, size, lymph nodes, and the estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2, which drugs can target; anti-estrogen therapy for an estrogen-receptor tumor. The prognosis of an invasive breast carcinoma depends on its histologic type (ductal or lobular), its size, the presence of lymph node metastases (the stage), and whether it expresses estrogen or progesterone receptors and the surface protein HER2. All of them can be targeted by specific drugs, so knowing a tumor's receptor and HER2 status guides the treatment: surgical excision, with or without chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and anti-estrogen therapy for a tumor that expresses estrogen receptors. In situ DCIS: needs treatment (surgery, with or without radiotherapy); good prognosis LCIS: neoplastic but benign (WHO); no treatment needed Invasive Forms little ducts or glands No glands; single files infiltrating the stroma 11 Chronic endometritis and the leiomyoma: plasma cells in the endometrium, a common cause of infertility treated with antibiotics; the leiomyoma, very common, a well-circumscribed nodule that makes the uterus bleed, against the aggressive leiomyosarcoma that spreads to the lung Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Chronic endometritis: plasma cells in the endometrial stroma, a common cause of infertility, treated with antibiotics. Chronic endometritis, inflammation of the endometrium, is benign and frequent, and one of the most common causes of infertility: a woman trying to get pregnant who looks healthy and has no symptoms. It can also cause abnormal uterine bleeding or pain. The physician samples the endometrium, and the pathologist finds plasma cells in the stroma. It is easily treated with antibiotics, and the patient can then get pregnant. The leiomyoma is the benign tumor of the uterine smooth muscle, and it is very frequent: the lecture said nearly every woman has some by perimenopause or after. Leiomyomas are white, elastic, very well-circumscribed nodules in the myometrium. "It's like having a foreign body in the midst of the myometrium": the myometrium can't contract well, so the usual symptom is excess, abnormal uterine bleeding. The malignant one, the leiomyosarcoma, is very aggressive and can metastasize to the lung very easily. 12 The ovary and the male breast: most ovarian tumors are epithelial, and ovarian cancer is lethal; gynecomastia (aromatase in fat, testosterone in weightlifters) is far more common than male breast cancer, which has no screening Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Most ovarian tumors are epithelial, from the surface; ovarian cancer is aggressive and lethal. The ovary gives rise to a plethora of tumors; the classification isn't needed ("Don't shoot me. I don't need you to know this"). Know that most ovarian tumors come from the surface epithelium (the epithelial tumors); others come from the germ cells (the germ cell tumors, as in the testis) and from the stroma. Ovarian cancer is lethal: it causes more deaths than its frequency would suggest, it is very aggressive, it needs a lot of chemotherapy and debulking surgery, and the prognosis isn't good. The male breast has the same pathology as the female breast, but its cancer is found later, because men have no mammography or screening: the cancer is so rare that a screening program isn't justified. Much more common is gynecomastia, an enlarged breast from excess estrogen: in obese men, whose fat has the aromatase that converts testosterone to estradiol, and in weightlifters who take testosterone. Also flagged in class The koilocyte, a bigger nucleus with a clear halo around it, is HPV's mark in cytology and biopsies. High-grade cells: less cytoplasm, a higher N:C ratio, pleomorphic nuclei. Lichen sclerosus: atrophic epithelium, dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, a parchment-like vulva; it leads to the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of older women. Paget disease of the nipple, a scaly red nipple of carcinoma cells, means looking for the carcinoma underneath.
